newsitem.title: CHINA: Stop arms sale to Taiwan, China tells U.S. general.
newsitem.headline: Stop arms sale to Taiwan, China tells U.S. general.

text.p: China's top brass has told U.S. General John Shalikashvili that the United States should stop selling advanced weapons to its rival, Taiwan, the China news service said on Thursday.

"The Chinese side hopes the U.S. side...will stop selling advanced weapons to Taiwan to prevent bad effects on relations between the two countries and their militaries," the agency quoted General Zhang Wannian as telling Shalikashvili, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff.
The United States has sold F-16 jet fighters, missiles and other weapons to Taiwan in recent years in the wake of the island's decision to embrace democratic reforms.
Beijing and Taipei have been rivals since the Communists won the Chinese civil war and sent the defeated Nationalists fleeing into exile on Taiwan in 1949.
Zhang, a vice-chairman of the ruling Communist Party's powerful Central Military Commission, said the two sides should be far-sighted and keep their common interests in mind. He did not elaborate.
Zhang told Shalikashvili that the United States should "handle the Taiwan problem appropriately...to maintain the trend of improving ties", the news agency said.
Sino-U.S. relations soured when Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui made a landmark, private trip to the United States in June 1995 in a bid to break out of diplomatic isolation imposed by China.

Ties further deteriorated in March 1996 when the United States sent two aircraft carrier battlegroups to waters near Taiwan to prevent Chinese war games and missile tests from disrupting the island's first presidential elections.
A series of visits to China by senior U.S. officials have helped to put delicate relations back on track.

On Wednesday, Shalikashvili told China's National Defence University that Washington wanted more Sino-U.S. exchanges and a military maritime and air cooperation agreement that would cut the risk of miscalculations.

Information exchange should be more equal, China's military should take part in multinational activities and a regular dialogue between senior military leaders should be introduced, Shalikashvili said, adding that improving contacts would be difficult.

Relations between the world's most powerful military machine and the three million-strong People's Liberation Army, the world's largest army, have slowly revived in recent years since being frozen in 1989 after Chinese soldiers crushed demonstrations for democracy in Beijing with heavy loss of life.
Shalikashvili is the most senior U.S. military officer to visit Beijing since 1983. He is scheduled to leave China on Friday.
